---
title: "Ten Rules for Reading Playtest Data"
subtitle: "The spine of the next three weeks"
---

> These ten rules are the spine of this module's analytics strand. Each one is
> unpacked in the notes that follow, and every lab will send you back to at least
> one of them. When a lab says *"rule 5 again"*, this is the page it means.

---

1. **Decide what would change your mind before you look at the data.**
   An analysis that cannot come out against you is not an analysis.

2. **A number without a question attached is decoration.**
   Ask the question first, in words, and in the form a designer would ask it.

3. **Know what kind of number you are holding.**
   You cannot average a category, and a 1–5 rating is not a measurement.

4. **Look at the shape before you quote the average.**
   Every summary throws information away; the shape tells you what was thrown.

5. **The mean is the wrong summary more often than you think.**
   Anything skewed — completion times, session lengths, frame times — belongs to
   the median.

6. **Cleaning is analysis.**
   Every row you drop is a decision with a consequence, and you must be able to
   say what it was.

7. **Compare distributions, not averages.**
   Two groups with the same mean can be completely different games.

8. **Small samples lie confidently.**
   Report how many people you measured, every time, in the same breath as the
   result.

9. **Sometimes the rare value is the whole story.**
   Averages hide stutter, crashes, and the one puzzle where everybody quits.

10. **A finding that does not name an action is not finished.**
    What -> Pattern -> Meaning -> Action.
